title: How far does a random walker get?
hook: Left or right on every coin flip. After 100 steps, does the walker go nowhere, or far?

doesNotKnow: that a random walk's distance from the start grows like the square root of the number of steps

misconception: A walker who goes left or right at random stays near where they started, or else drifts in proportion to the number of steps.
objective: The learner can explain that random steps partly but not fully cancel, so the typical distance grows like the square root of the steps: about 8 m after 100 steps, about 25 m after 1,000.

claims.text: After 100 random 1 m steps, a walker ends on average about 8 m from the start.
claims.source: Exact E|S_100| from the binomial distribution = 7.96 (exactMeanDist() in src/demos/probability/drunk-walk-distance/model.ts); approximation sqrt(2n/pi) = 7.98.

claims.text: After 1,000 steps the average distance is about 25 m: ten times the steps gives only about three times the distance.
Spread grows like the square root of the number of steps, so 100 times the steps gives 10 times the distance.
claims.source: Position is a sum of n independent +1/-1 steps with variance 1 each: SD = sqrt(n); E|S_n| ~ sqrt(2n/pi). Both scale with sqrt(n).

claims.text: The stage's first 30 walkers averaged 2.8 m, 7.3 m and 24.9 m from the start after 10, 100 and 1,000 steps.
claims.source: walkers() in model.ts, seed 1921, untuned (the first seed tried). Over 500 other batches of 30 walkers the average distance at 100 steps had middle 95% 5.9-10.4 m (median 7.9); at 1,000 steps 19.2-32.7 m (median 25.4).

recall.question: A random walker is on average about 10 m from the start after some number of steps. Roughly how far after 100 times as many steps?
recall.why: Distance grows like the square root of the steps: 100 times the steps gives sqrt(100) = 10 times the distance.
